steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $14,600 from web design (2 clients). Interest $1,780 (Synchrony Bank), dividends $440 (Interactive Brokers). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,820/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (Sallie Mae, 2017–2020); charity $2,000 to Boston Medical Center (donation, have receipt) have the receipt; unreimbursed expenses $950. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
I can help — this looks straightforward but I need a couple quick clarifications before I run numbers. Summary below of how things work, what forms to use, and the items I’ll need to produce an accurate comparison (standard vs itemized) and the best home-office treatment.

Quick clarifying questions
- Is the $4,400 in “student loan interest” the amount you actually paid in 2024, or is that an aggregate from earlier years (2017–2020)? Only interest paid in the tax year matters for the deduction. Do you have a 1098‑E for 2024 and the amount on it?
- Are the $950 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for your web‑design work (i.e., self‑employment expenses), or are they employee unreimbursed expenses from a W‑2 job? (Employee unreimbursed job expenses are not deductible for most taxpayers.)
- Do you (or your spouse) receive any other income or adjustments (e.g., retirement distributions, many 1099s, student loan interest paid by spouse, etc.)?
- Were the two web‑design clients issuing 1099‑NEC / 1099‑MISC / 1099‑K? (I only need this for reporting completeness — you still report gross receipts even without 1099s.)

Federal tax treatment — overview (high level)
- Filing status: Married filing jointly. 2024 standard deduction for MFJ is $29,200.
- Income to report: W‑2 wages ($82,350), self‑employment gross receipts ($14,600), interest ($1,780), ordinary dividends ($440). All are included in gross income.
- Student loan interest: If you paid interest in 2024, you may be able to deduct up to $2,500 as an adjustment to income (on Schedule 1), subject to MAGI phaseouts. That deduction reduces AGI (unlike charitable giving which is an itemized deduction).
- Charitable contribution: $2,000 (you have a receipt). This is an itemized deduction on Schedule A.
- Unreimbursed expenses: If they are business expenses for your side gig, include them on Schedule C. If they are unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job, those generally are not deductible under current law.
- Home office: Because you have self‑employment income, you can claim a home‑office deduction. You have two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5 per square foot up to 300 sq ft. For 155 sq ft that’s 155 × $5 = $775 (easy and no Form 8829).
  - Regular method (recommended to consider because it’s likely larger for you): compute the business percentage = home office sq ft / total sq ft = 155 / 680 ≈ 22.8%. Apply that percentage to allocable home expenses (rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.). Example: rent $1,820/mo → $21,840/yr × 22.8% ≈ $4,977. That amount (and a share of utilities) is deductible on Schedule C as business expense. If you use the regular method you generally use Form 8829 to compute the business‑use-of‑home deduction.
  - Important limitations: home‑office deduction for self‑employed reduces your net profit on Schedule C. The regular method cannot produce a business loss that is limited/brought forward beyond net self‑employment income (excess expenses may carry forward to the next year).
- Self‑employment tax: Net profit from Schedule C is subject to self‑employment tax (Social Security + Medicare). You calculate it on Schedule SE. You can deduct half of self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1), which lowers AGI.
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: You may be eligible for up to 20% of qualified business income from your web design (reported via Form 8995 or 8995‑A) — this can further reduce taxable income. Eligibility depends on taxable income level and type of business; with your numbers you’re likely under phaseout thresholds and should get some QBI benefit.
- Itemize vs standard: Compare total itemized deductions (Schedule A) to the standard deduction ($29,200 for MFJ). With the items you listed (charity $2,000, no mortgage interest, no large state/local taxes listed), your itemized total will likely be far below the standard deduction. However, the home‑office deduction is NOT an itemized deduction — it reduces Schedule C net profit, so it effectively reduces AGI/taxable income regardless of whether you take the standard deduction. That means you should still likely use the standard deduction but also claim the home‑office deduction on Schedule C (regular method if larger).
- Records: Keep receipts, 1098‑E (student loan interest), 1099‑INT / 1099‑DIV, any 1099‑NEC or records of client payments, and documentation for home office (photo, floor plan, how you calculated square footage, rent/utility bills).

Which forms to use (federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 — for adjustments to income (student loan interest deduction, half of SE tax is an adjustment).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report web‑design income and business expenses, and include home‑office expenses here (or via Form 8829).
- Form 8829 — if you use the regular method to compute business use of home. (Not used with simplified method.)
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — to claim the QBI (20%) deduction if eligible.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (likely unnecessary given the $29,200 MFJ standard deduction unless you have other itemizable amounts).
- State: Arizona individual return (AZ Form 140 or the current AZ return form for 2024) — state rules may differ; AZ generally conforms closely but confirm state-specific credits/deductions.

Estimated comparison (illustrative) — assuming two things:
- The $4,400 is NOT paid in 2024 (so assume student loan interest paid in 2024 is $2,500 or you qualify for the full $2,500 max), and
- The $950 unreimbursed expenses are business expenses.

I can run a quick estimate now if you confirm the actual student‑loan interest amount paid in 2024 and confirm the $950 are business expenses. But as an illustration:
- Regular home‑office allocation of rent (22.8% of annual rent) ≈ $4,977 (plus share of utilities if you want more accuracy). That substantially reduces self‑employment net profit.
- Simplified home‑office = $775.
- Using the regular method in the illustration yields a notably lower taxable income than the simplified method (because rent allocation is large relative to simplified amount).

Next steps — what I can do for you
- If you confirm (a) how much student loan interest you paid in 2024 (and whether you have Form 1098‑E), and (b) whether the $950 is business expense, I will:
  - Produce a side‑by‑side numeric comparison (simplified vs regular home‑office methods) showing net self‑employment profit, self‑employment tax, AGI, taxable income (standard vs itemized), and rough federal tax estimate.
  - Tell you which exact federal forms and lines to fill and what to report on AZ return.
  - Give a short checklist of documents to keep and what to give a preparer/CPA.
- If you want, I can draft an email to your CPA with the summarized facts and ask for any missing items — I can prepare that and either draft or send it for you.

Which would you like me to do now? If “run the numbers,” please confirm the student‑loan interest paid in 2024 and whether the $950 are business expenses.
